Summary (auto): quick notes — discussed OTEL collector config, token-level metrics, how KV cache shows up in traces, batching behaviour, and on-prem/VPC network constraints. Action items captured separately.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining i'm alex from Redwood, today priya and i will run through how we expose token-level metrics and traces and how that works with a vpc/on-prem setup
[00:10] Martin Lopez: thanks alex, we had a few pre-reads but want to focus on operational visibility — we need to see per-request token costs and cache behavior in our dashboards, also compliance questions for kms
[00:25] Priya Kapoor: great, we'll start with the data model — the runtime emits metrics at token granularity: tokens_generated, tokens_cached, latency_ms per decode step, and batch_size. we also attach attributes: model.variant, seq_length, request_id, customer_tier, hardware (gpu_type)
[00:45] Sana Patel: when you say token-level, do you mean an actual metric per token? that will be a lot of series
[00:55] Priya Kapoor: great question, it's mostly histogramed and aggregated. we export counters for tokens_generated and tokens_cached then have derived metrics like cache_hit_rate. we also emit summaries for latency and a per-request span with child spans for kv_cache lookup and decode
[01:15] Lee Wong: how do we correlate spans to metrics? we want to be able to trace a slow tail to either batching or cache misses
[01:25] Priya Kapoor: we put the same request_id as a trace/span attribute and as a label on metrics. so the dashboard can link traces to metric time series. we use OTEL semantics — you can search Tempo/Jaeger for the request id and see the span tree
[01:40] Martin Lopez: is that OTLP over TLS from inside our vpc? we prefer not to open egress to public collectors
[01:50] Alex Chen: yes, in VPC/on‑prem we support pushing to a self-hosted OTEL collector behind a VPC endpoint. the collector can live in your network and forward to your observability stack (OTLP/gRPC or http). we also provide a small example collector config in the repo
[02:05] Sana Patel: can you show the collector config? any special batching or resource needs?
[02:12] Priya Kapoor: yeah i'll share. key bits: enable memory_limiter, set batch_size to align with our token emission (so you don't flood the collector), and use the otlp exporter with tls and client certs if you want mTLS. example config: receiver otlp -> batch processor -> prometheus exporter + otlp exporter to your backend
[02:35] Alex Chen: note that for very high token rates we recommend running a local prometheus remote_write or using a buffered gateway, otherwise you can get backpressure. also we advise 2-3 collector replicas with modest CPU for heavy workloads
[02:50] Martin Lopez: what's the overhead of the tracing itself on latency? we can't add too much tail latency
[02:58] Priya Kapoor: tracing spans are lightweight. default sampling is 1% for high qps, but for pilot we can sample 100% for investigation. most heavy work is in metric aggregation, not the span emission. worst case we saw ~2-5ms added on p99 when all instrumentation enabled, but that was with a very aggressive 100% sampling and pushing spans synchronously
[03:23] Lee Wong: how about the KV cache — can you show how it appears in traces?
[03:30] Priya Kapoor: sure, kv_cache is a child span of the request span. attributes include cache_hit (true/false), cache_key, cache_latency_ms and kv_cache_size. when a hit occurs we'll increment tokens_cached for the request and annotate the span with cached_tokens count
[03:50] Martin Lopez: okay so we can filter traces where cache_hit=false to find misses that are causing latency?
[03:55] Priya Kapoor: exactly, and on dashboards you can graph cache_hit_rate over time and tie that to model_variant or seq_length to see where caching helps most
[04:10] Alex Chen: quick note on quantization — when you run quantized models (4-bit etc) you'll reduce decode time per token but also change memory access patterns, so attribute model.quantized=true is included. priya can share recommended quantization profiles per model
[04:30] Priya Kapoor: yeah we'll send profiles. also when quantized and using KV caching, hit latencies are often lower but cpu/GPU utilization patterns differ — important to include gpu_util and mem_bandwidth attributes in metrics
[04:50] Sana Patel: for dashboards, do you provide pre-built Grafana dashboards? we use Grafana/Tempo/Loki stack on-prem
[04:58] Alex Chen: we have a dashboard JSON you can import that includes token-level charts, cache heatmaps, batching-size distributions, and per-model latency percentiles. we'll attach it. it's designed to work with Prometheus + Tempo traces
[05:15] Martin Lopez: security: KMS integration and audit logs — we need to ensure model keys never leave our HSM. how does Redwood handle key management in private deployment?
[05:26] Alex Chen: in private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. Redwood's control plane can be run in a customer VPC and use IAM roles to access the KMS endpoint, keys never exported. we also emit audit logs for model changes and rollout events to your syslog/S3 for compliance
[05:45] Sana Patel: do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for the console and the collector admin UI?
[05:50] Priya Kapoor: yes, SAML and OIDC are supported, RBAC for roles (admin, viewer, ops). audit trails are retained per your retention settings; for SOC2 customers we can extend retention and provide manual evidence bundles
[06:05] Lee Wong: what's the recommended metric cardinality strategy? token-level with model.variant and request_id will explode series
[06:15] Priya Kapoor: we avoid putting request_id on every metric; request_id is a trace attribute. metrics use lower-cardinality labels: model.variant, seq_bucket (short/med/long), region, hardware_type. token-level counters are aggregated, not per-request. traces are used for high-cardinality debugging
[06:35] Martin Lopez: demo time? maybe a quick walkthrough of a trace that shows a cache miss causing a p99 spike
[06:40] Priya Kapoor: yes i'll share screen, sorry audio is a bit laggy for me, let me paste a sample trace id... [Priya pastes trace id]
[07:05] Priya Kapoor: here's a trace: request -> routing -> batching -> kv_cache (miss) -> decode. kv_cache span shows 18ms latency, decode span 320ms. on the metric side tokens_cached for the interval was low, and batch_size spiked to 16 which actually increased tail latency here
[07:35] Alex Chen: that's typical: batching helps throughput but can hurt p99 if your arrival distribution is spiky. we recommend dynamic batching with queue thresholds and burst capacity in dedicated pools
[07:50] Lee Wong: you mentioned queue thresholds — do you expose queue length as a metric?
[07:55] Priya Kapoor: yes, queue_length and queue_wait_time are emitted per serving pool. combine that with batch_size histogram and you can set adaptive autoscaling thresholds
[08:10] Sana Patel: for our pilot, we'll probably run in our VPC first then move to a private deployment. what's the smallest footprint we can start with?
[08:20] Alex Chen: you can start with a 2-GPU node pool for low throughput dev pilot, but for realistic perf testing use 4+ GPUs with one dedicated collector and a prometheus remote_write setup. we'll help with sizing based on your expected RPS and token/req distribution
[08:40] Martin Lopez: what about cost visibility at token level? we need per-route cost breakdown
[08:48] Priya Kapoor: runtime emits token counters per-route and per-model variant. Redwood Console charges and cost attribution can be exported; for private you can ingest the same metrics and compute cost per token using a small script we'll provide
[09:05] Alex Chen: quick note on fallback behavior in hybrid deployments — we annotate traces when a request falls back to a smaller model variant, and emit attribute fallback=true and fallback_reason. helpful for understanding quality regressions after autoscale events
[09:25] Lee Wong: are there any Gotchas for on-prem network rules with OTLP/gRPC? we've had issues with intermittent connection resets
[09:32] Priya Kapoor: gRPC is sensitive to idle timeouts on middleboxes. recommend keepalive and retry settings in the collector. also if you use TLS mTLS ensure the proxies pass client certs; otherwise fall back to file-based SUVs for cert rotation
[09:50] Martin Lopez: ok thanks. can we run a benchmark that compares quantized 4-bit with and without KV cache and measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and GPU util?
[09:59] Priya Kapoor: yes, priya will run that and include the OTEL metrics and traces in the run so you can replay the dashboards
[10:10] Alex Chen: last bit on long-term ops — we recommend alerting on sudden drops in cache_hit_rate, spikes in queue_wait_time, and increases in tokens_generated per route. we'll share suggested alert rules for Grafana/Prometheus
[10:25] Martin Lopez: great, that helps. anything else on compliance?
[10:30] Alex Chen: we'll send SOC2 docs and the private deployment security whitepaper. for HSM/KMS integration I'll include example IAM policies and an architecture diagram for the keyflow.
[10:40] Priya Kapoor: and i'll attach the collector config and dashboard JSON in the follow-up email.
[10:50] Martin Lopez: perfect, thanks both. quick recap — alex will send security docs and dashboard, priya will run benchmark and send collector configs, we (nexa) will share topology and KMS details. target follow-up week of 2026-12-28 to review results and next steps
[11:05] Alex Chen: thanks all!
[11:10] (meeting ends)
